passage: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage
text:
The narrator's husband John mocks her suspicion that the house is strange, and she accepts such teasing as a normal part of married life. The line shows her dry, self-aware tone and her sense that she is dismissed.

The narrator has just said there is "something queer" about the house, asking why it is rented so cheaply and has stood empty so long. Her remark that John laughs at her "of course" suggests this is a routine pattern between them, not a single quarrel. p. 1

The phrase "one expects that in marriage" is ironic: she treats his ridicule as a conventional husband's habit, which hints at the wider theme of a woman whose perceptions are repeatedly brushed aside by the men around her. p. 1

passage: I am sitting by the window now, up in this atrocious nursery
text: The narrator is writing at a window in the upstairs nursery, which she calls "atrocious," and she says nothing stops her writing except her lack of strength. The selected line comes from the opening of page 3, where the narrator reflects on being able to write freely now that her husband John is away. Her word choice signals her growing hostility toward the room, especially its wallpaper, which the reader will soon see as the centre of her distress. The contrast between the freedom to write and her weakness hints at the tension between her wish for work and the rest imposed on her, a theme the story develops throughout.

passage: It is the same woman, I know, for she is always creeping
text:
The narrator is certain the figure she keeps seeing outside is the same woman each time, because that woman is always creeping. The selected line is one she uses to justify her belief in a single, recurring figure.

The line sits in a passage where she describes seeing the creeping woman from every window: on the shaded lane, in the grape arbors, and under the trees on the road. Her reasoning is that the figure's constant creeping makes it one person, and that most women do not creep in daylight, which makes the sight strange and unsettling. The claim is built on what she sees, not on anything another character confirms.

Within the story, this is central to the narrator's unraveling. The woman she sees outside is linked to the figure she has traced behind the yellow wallpaper, so the line reinforces her growing identification with the trapped woman. The passage is narrated by someone whose perceptions are increasingly distorted, so the reader should weigh her certainty skeptically.

passage: I think that woman gets out in the daytime
text:
The narrator has come to believe that the woman she sees behind the wallpaper escapes into the open world during daylight. This is the clearest sign yet of how far her fixation has taken her.

The line sits on page 10, just after she has reasoned that the figure shakes the pattern and tries to climb through it, with the pattern strangling those who try. Her conclusion that the woman escapes by day follows from that picture, and it links the paper to the outside world she is otherwise kept from.

Her reasoning is private and unsupported, which is what makes it unsettling. She is shut in a room, watched by a husband who treats her illness as imagined, and her belief that a trapped woman is roaming free mirrors her own confinement. The passage's notation is simply the narrator's own voice and syntax, so there are no symbols or equations to explain.

passage: send me to Weir Mitchell in the fall
text:
The passage is a fictional first-person narrative, so there is no factual claim to test here. The narrator, confined to a nursery room with a yellow wallpaper, records her husband John's view that she is merely suffering from temporary nervous depression, and his threat to send her to Weir Mitchell in the fall. The document offers no experiments, data or citations in support of its claims, only the narrator's own perceptions and John's medical opinions within the story.

passage: Personally, I disagree with their ideas
text:
The narrator's disagreement is only asserted, so a critic could say she offers no reasoned case against the rest cure, and that her own unreliable state makes her judgment suspect.

A careful critic would note that the narrator's rejection of her physicians rests on feeling rather than evidence. She simply states that "congenial work, with excitement and change, would do me good," yet she also concedes that she is "nervous" and prone to "fancies," which her husband and brother read as symptoms. A reader who takes the medical view seriously could argue that her opposition is itself a symptom of the condition the doctors describe, so her disagreement counts for little as testimony. The text gives no data on either side, so the claim that work would help her is untested.

The author's best reply, as the text itself implies, is that the narrator is denied any outlet for her ideas, since she is forbidden to work and must hide what she does write, so her disagreement is the only evidence of her own needs that the story allows.

passage: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage
text:
The line reads as affectionate teasing, but it may be the first sign of a marriage in which the narrator's perceptions are dismissed.

The narrator presents the laughter as harmless and expected, since "one expects that in marriage." Yet on this same page John is "practical in the extreme," has "no patience with faith," and "scoffs openly at any talk of things not to be felt and seen and put down in figures" p. 1. Read alongside that description, the laughter looks less like play and more like a steady refusal to take her seriously. The narrator's ready acceptance of it is what makes her account worth questioning, because she has already absorbed his view that her feelings are not reliable evidence.

The narrator's own wry, affectionate tone supports the lighter reading, and the text leaves the judgment about John to the reader.

passage: I have locked the door and thrown the key down into the front path
question: Why does she throw the key away?
text:
The narrator gives her own reason right after the line: she doesn't want to go out, and she doesn't want anyone to come in until John arrives, because she wants to astonish him p. 12. Locking herself in secures the time she needs to finish stripping the paper and to "get back behind the pattern" at night, without Jennie or the servants interrupting.

The key also becomes a tool in the final scene. When John pounds at the door, she calmly tells him where it is, under a plantain leaf, and repeats it until he goes to fetch it p. 12 p. 13. That keeps him away long enough for her to be found already "out," as she puts it.

The text doesn't spell out any deeper motive. Reading the gesture as a deliberate cutting of the link to the outside world, or as her taking control after being managed so closely, is interpretation rather than something the document states. Earlier she says John "takes all care from me" and gives her a schedule for each hour p. 2, so the contrast is available to a reader.

passage: He says that with my imaginative power and habit of story-making
question: Is John right about her imagination?
text:
The document doesn't settle this directly, and John's claim is really two claims: that she has a strong imagination, and that it is dangerous to her health.

The first has some support. She mentions her childhood habit of finding "entertainment and terror" in blank walls and furniture, and of seeing a kindly wink in the knobs of a bureau p. 4. She also admits she always fancies she sees people walking in the garden paths p. 3. Her writing is another sign of a story-making mind.

The second is where the story undercuts him. His remedy is to forbid writing, company, and stimulation, and to have her think about her condition as little as possible. Yet she says congenial work would do her good p. 1, and she finds the wallpaper dwells in her mind because nothing else does. As she grows more isolated, her fancies grow from the wallpaper's eyes into the woman behind the pattern p. 7. The text suggests his treatment feeds the very tendency he warns against, though the narrator never states that conclusion herself. Whether a different approach would have helped is outside what the document tells us.

passage: It is the same woman, I know, for she is always creeping
question: Who is the woman in the wallpaper?
text:
The document never says outright who she is, so what follows is interpretation. Within the story, the narrator first makes out "a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern" p. 7, and by this page she believes the figure shakes the bars of the pattern and tries to climb through p. 10. She also sees "the same woman" creeping outside, in the lane, the arbors, and along the road p. 10. Her reason for thinking it is one woman is simply that she is always creeping.

The text hints at a connection between the two. The woman is trapped behind bars, much as the narrator is confined to a barred nursery under John's schedule, and the narrator is hiding and creeping by daylight herself p. 10. The streak around the wall, which her shoulder later fits, suggests someone has crept there before p. 12. The ending, where she says "I've got out at last" p. 13, merges the two.

From general knowledge, most critics read the woman as the narrator's own suppressed self, and as a figure for women confined by the domestic and medical expectations of the period.

question: Who is Jennie and how does she treat the narrator?
text:
Jennie is a household helper who looks after the house and the narrator, and she appears to be John's sister. The narrator calls her "John's sister," a "dear girl" and "a perfect, and enthusiastic housekeeper" p. 4. Later the narrator says "Jennie sees to everything now" p. 5, and Jennie is the one who will get the house ready for their return p. 7. The document never states outright that Jennie and the sister are the same person, so that identification is an inference from the context.

On the surface Jennie is kind and careful. She is "good and lets me alone when I want her to" p. 5. The narrator suspects her, though. She believes Jennie is secretly studying the wallpaper, and Jennie explains she was touching it because it stains clothes p. 8, p. 9. Jennie also reports to John that the narrator sleeps a good deal in the daytime p. 11. The narrator reads this as betrayal, though from the text it looks like ordinary concern. Near the end Jennie offers to sleep with her and to help her rest, and the narrator treats this as slyness p. 11. Whether Jennie is truly guarded or just worried is something the narrator's account can't settle.

question: How does the narrator's view of the wallpaper change over the story?
text:
The narrator's view moves from disgust, to obsession, to identification.

At first she finds the paper simply hideous. She calls it "one of those sprawling flamboyant patterns committing every artistic sin" and its color "repellant, almost revolting" p. 2. She says she would hate it herself if she had to live with it, and she wants it replaced p. 3.

Then it becomes a puzzle that holds her. She admits she is "getting really fond of the room in spite of the wallpaper. Perhaps because of the wallpaper" and follows the pattern for hours p. 5. She starts to see a figure behind the front design, which she decides is "like a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern" p. 7. By night the outer pattern becomes bars and the woman is plain p. 8.

Next it turns into a secret she guards. She feels better because of it, and refuses to leave until she has "found it out" p. 9. She also grows suspicious of John and Jennie for looking at it p. 8.

Finally she sees herself as the woman. She helps peel the paper to free her p. 11, and at the end declares "I've got out at last" p. 13. The wallpaper is no longer an object she hates but the place she lives and creeps.

question: Why does John faint at the end, and what does the narrator's last line suggest?
text:
The document never says why John faints. The narrator herself asks, "Now why should that man have fainted?" p. 13. Any explanation is interpretation, and the text supports a few.

The most direct reading is shock. He breaks in expecting a patient he has been treating for "temporary nervous depression" p. 1, and finds her creeping along the wall, claiming "I've got out at last," with the paper pulled off p. 13. His cry, "For God's sake, what are you doing!", shows he is horrified p. 13. He has insisted all along that she was improving and that her fears were "a false and foolish fancy" p. 7, so the scene overturns his confidence as a physician. The narrator's own account also adds the cruel detail that she has to step over him.

Her last line, that she "had to creep over him every time," suggests a reversal of power p. 13. John has controlled her schedule, her rooms, her writing and her visitors. Now he lies prone in her path, and she is indifferent to him. That can be read as a triumphant liberation or as a complete breakdown, and the story leaves both open. Her freedom is also only inside the room, since she is still creeping in the smooch along the wall p. 12.

A woman, confined by her physician husband to a rented summer mansion for a supposed nervous condition, keeps a secret journal. Her fixation on the yellow wallpaper of her nursery room grows as the story moves through the summer.

Where we are

A couple rent a secluded colonial mansion for the summer; the narrator is forbidden to work and told to rest because of her "nervous depression." p. 1
They live in a former nursery at the top of the house, with barred windows, a bed fixed in place and peeling, repellent yellow wallpaper. p. 2
The narrator writes in secret, since her husband and his sister disapprove. The rental runs three months, so time is limited. p. 7

People

The narrator — Unnamed writer of the journal, a wife and new mother, treated as an invalid and cut off from work and company.
John — Her husband, a practical physician who dismisses her fears and directs her every hour.
Jennie — John's sister, a devoted housekeeper who looks after the household and the narrator.
Mary — The nurse who cares for the narrator's baby.
Her brother — Also a physician, who agrees with John's diagnosis of her condition.

Threads to watch

Her own sense of her illness and need for meaningful work clashes with the rest cure her husband and brother insist on. p. 1
The wallpaper's pattern, and a figure behind it, take over her attention. Watch how her account of what she sees changes. p. 7
She hides her writing, her wakefulness and her thoughts from John, while he and Jennie seem increasingly watchful of her. p. 8
The narrator's trust in John is strained as she asks to leave and is refused, with the lease ending in weeks. p. 7
